title: lncRNA loci with a published growth claim drop out more than matched controls in three human screens, but the claimed direction predicts nothing detectable
abstract:
Long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) loci that a paper says are needed for the growth of a human cancer cell line do lose cells faster than comparable loci in genome-scale knock-down screens, but loci whose papers claim the opposite effect behave the same way, so we find no sign that these screens respond to what was published rather than to which loci were studied. This matters because the low rate at which such screens confirm published lncRNA work is widely used as evidence that most non-coding DNA function is not real, and that argument needs a measuring instrument shown to track whether a claim is true.

We took statements of the form 'gene G is needed for the growth of cell line L' from PubMed abstracts and looked up what three public screens measured for G in L: a Cas13d screen of 5,496 lncRNAs and 3,156 protein-coding genes in 5 cell lines, a CasRx screen of 24,171 lncRNA loci in 6 lines, and a CRISPRi screen in 5 lines. For each claim we expressed the screen's log fold change as a percentile among the 50 nearest loci in expression, excluding claimed loci; 0.5 means no information. Claimed lncRNA loci reached 0.435 (95% confidence interval 0.389 to 0.482) in the Cas13d screen, with 2.2 times the expected number of hits. Claims in the opposite direction scored alike: the difference between directions was -0.012 (-0.102 to +0.078) for Cas13d, +0.006 (-0.034 to +0.047) for CasRx and +0.027 (-0.078 to +0.136) for CRISPRi, and contrary-direction claims were hits as often as same-direction claims. Published claims about protein-coding genes behaved like lncRNA claims under one shared protocol (difference -0.017, -0.086 to +0.053). The excess sat at lncRNA loci that also contain a small-RNA gene: 38% to 67% of the claimed loci the screens flag are such loci, against 6% to 13% expected. We also measured the test's limit: a locus called a hit in two or more other cell lines reaches only 0.318 (Cas13d) or 0.157 (CasRx) in the line being measured.

Limits: the direction result is an absence of evidence, and no interval excludes the possibility that the published direction carries the whole observed signal, so no single claim is confirmed or refuted here; claims come from abstracts (direction correct in 86% of a blind audit); the Cas13d result rests mostly on one cell line; half of claimed lncRNAs are below 1 transcript per million in the named line. Two rounds of independent review changed the analysis and the claims. We state a re-screening test of the main finding.

display.caption: Mean drop-out percentile of published growth claims in genome-scale screens of the same cell lines, with 95% bootstrap intervals over genes. 0.5 means the claim carries no information beyond the locus's expression level. Blue: papers claiming the locus supports growth, so that losing it should slow growth. Orange: papers claiming the locus restrains growth, so that losing it should speed growth. The two directions score alike in every screen and in both gene classes. The intervals are wide: this is an absence of evidence that the published direction predicts the screen, not a demonstration that it cannot.

The same statistic for claimed lncRNA loci, split by whether the locus also contains a small-RNA gene (snoRNA, miRNA, scaRNA or snRNA) on the same strand, from GENCODE v44 plus the UCSC wgRna track. Such loci are 2.6% of lncRNA genes but 1.9 to 4.8 times over-represented among claimed loci relative to an expression- and guide-matched expectation. The difference between the two groups is clear in 3 of the 6 sets shown.

Expression of lncRNAs with a published growth claim, in the cell line the paper names, against all lncRNA loci the screens tested in the same lines. Claimed lncRNAs are more abundant than average, but 64% are still below 1 transcript per million, where an RNA-targeting screen has little power.

citations.reason: We reuse its reading of the Liang et al. Cas13d screen tables and its finding that calls concentrate at small-RNA host loci and that single-line calls are mostly false; our yardstick is built on reproducible hits because of it.
We adapt its PubMed retrieval and HGNC-based gene-name resolution code for extracting claims from abstracts.
Independent evidence that selection on lncRNA splice sites is undetectable, consistent with our finding that claimed lncRNA loci without a small-RNA gene show no screen signal.

Closest prior work: a meta-analysis of the hepatocellular carcinoma lncRNA literature that compares lncRNAs with protein-coding genes. It judges claims by patient-tissue expression and has no direction control; we judge them by loss-of-function fitness in the cell lines the papers name.
The Cas13d screen whose gene-level results and RNA-seq we analyse.

The CRISPRi lncRNA screen, analysed through the gene-level re-analysis of Montero et al.
Comment on confounders of lncRNA knock-down screens; repeats and pseudogene homology are an alternative route to an excess at claimed loci that we do not model.
